sections.title: Introduction to Control Systems Security
sections.description: Defining control system cybersecurity, trends, potential consequences, malware events, and differences between IT and IACS

topics.title: Defining Control System Cybersecurity
topics.definition: Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computer systems and networks from unauthorized access, attacks, and damage.
topics.explanation: In simple terms, cybersecurity for control systems means putting locks and guards around the computers that run factories, power plants, and other critical infrastructure. Just like you protect your home with locks and alarms, organisations protect their control systems with digital security measures.
keyPoints: Measures to protect against unauthorized access
Electronic Security: Actions to protect critical systems from unauthorized use, denial of service, modifications, disclosure, loss of revenue, destruction
Control system: Hardware and software components of an Industrial Automation and Control System (IACS)
examples: A manufacturing plant uses cybersecurity to prevent hackers from stopping the production line
A power utility protects its grid from attacks that could cause blackouts
A water treatment facility secures its systems to ensure clean water delivery

tierCorrelations.level0: Process layer - Physical equipment being controlled
tierCorrelations.level1: Basic Control - Local controllers protecting equipment
tierCorrelations.level2: Supervisory Control - SCADA systems monitoring operations

topics.title: Trends in Control System Cybersecurity
topics.definition: Current patterns and developments in how control systems are being attacked and how they're evolving.
topics.explanation: The cybersecurity landscape is constantly changing. More attacks are happening, systems are becoming more connected, and new vulnerabilities are discovered regularly. Understanding these trends helps organisations stay ahead of threats.
keyPoints: Increased attacks on control systems
Use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) software and hardware
Common use of Internet Protocols (IP)
Increased use of remote monitoring and access
Availability of automated attack tools
Remote access broadens systems' attack surface
More published vulnerabilities in IACS components
examples: Ransomware attacks targeting hospitals and utilities
Remote work increasing exposure to cyber threats
Attackers using publicly available hacking tools
Supply chain attacks affecting multiple organisations
topics.examTips: Know the five main trends: increased attacks, COTS usage, IP protocols, remote access, and attack automation

topics.title: Potential Consequences
topics.definition: The negative outcomes that can result from a successful cyber attack on a control system.
topics.explanation: When a control system is compromised, the consequences can be severe - affecting not just the organisation but potentially people's safety and society as a whole.
keyPoints: Unauthorized access, theft, or misuse of data
Loss of integrity or reliability of the control system
Loss of availability and operational disruption
Equipment and reputational damage
Personal injury or loss of life
Financial losses and loss of competitive advantage
Violation of legal and regulatory requirements
organisationalImpact: Loss of customer trust and brand damage
societalImpact: Disruption of critical services (healthcare, transportation, utilities)
Psychological and physical harm to citizens

topics.title: Malware Trends
topics.definition: Patterns in malicious software attacks targeting control systems.
topics.explanation: Malware is malicious software designed to harm systems. In control systems, malware can cause physical damage to equipment, disrupt operations, or steal sensitive information. Ransomware is particularly concerning because attackers lock data and demand payment.
keyPoints: Ransomware: Attackers encrypt data and demand payment to restore access
Malware knows no borders - spreads worldwide regardless of location
Ransomware has become one of the highest cybersecurity threats
DDoS attacks combined with ransomware create compound threats
Rise of ransomware led to new government policies and initiatives
historicalExamples: Stuxnet (2010): Attacked Iran's nuclear centrifuges, showed vulnerability of critical infrastructure
WannaCry (2017): Global ransomware attack affecting hospitals and businesses
NotPetya (2017): Destructive malware targeting Ukraine, spreading globally
Colonial Pipeline (2021): Ransomware attack disrupted fuel supply across US East Coast
topics.examTips: Remember: Ransomware is a major threat, malware spreads globally, and historical attacks show real-world impact

sections.title: Awareness
sections.description: The role of human awareness and training in cybersecurity

topics.title: Security Awareness Fundamentals
topics.definition: Understanding and recognizing security threats and best practices in daily work.
topics.explanation: Most security breaches happen because people don't recognize threats or don't follow security procedures. Awareness training teaches employees to spot phishing emails, use strong passwords, and report suspicious activity.
keyPoints: Employees are often the weakest link in security
Awareness training reduces human error
Regular training keeps security top-of-mind
Reporting suspicious activity is everyone's responsibility
bestPractices: Verify requests before providing sensitive information
Report suspicious emails or activities immediately
Use strong, unique passwords for each system
Lock your computer when stepping away
Don't click links or download attachments from unknown sources

referenceModel.title: Purdue Reference Model for Control Hierarchies
referenceModel.description: The Purdue Model organizes industrial control systems into five hierarchical levels, each with specific security requirements and functions.

levels.name: Process
levels.description: Physical equipment and processes being controlled
levels.definition: The actual machinery, sensors, and physical systems that perform the work (e.g., motors, pumps, valves, conveyor belts).
levels.explanation: This is the 'bottom' level where physical work happens. Think of it as the factory floor equipment. At this level, you have sensors measuring temperature, pressure, flow rates, and actuators controlling equipment. Security here means protecting these devices from tampering or unauthorized control.
levels.systems: Sensors, actuators, motors, pumps, valves, PLCs (Programmemable Logic Controllers)
levels.securityFocus: Physical security, device authentication, preventing unauthorized commands
examples: Temperature sensors in a chemical reactor
Electric motors driving a conveyor belt
Pressure relief valves in a pipeline
Robotic arms in manufacturing

levels.name: Basic Control
levels.definition: Controllers that directly manage equipment at the process level, making real-time decisions based on sensor inputs.
levels.explanation: These are the 'brains' of individual machines. They receive data from sensors, make decisions, and send commands to equipment. A PLC (Programmemable Logic Controller) is a common example. At this level, security means ensuring only authorized commands reach the equipment.
levels.systems: PLCs, Distributed Control Systems (DCS), Remote Terminal Units (RTUs)
levels.securityFocus: Device authentication, secure communication with sensors/actuators, firmware integrity
examples: A PLC controlling a packaging machine
An RTU managing a water pump station
A DCS module controlling a chemical process

levels.name: Supervisory Control
levels.description: Systems monitoring and optimizing operations across multiple controllers
levels.definition: Higher-level systems that collect data from multiple controllers, display it to operators, and allow supervisory control of processes.
levels.explanation: SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems live here. They monitor what's happening across the entire facility, let operators see the big picture, and allow them to make adjustments. Security at this level is critical because compromising SCADA can affect many processes simultaneously.
levels.systems: SCADA systems, HMI (Human-Machine Interfaces), data historians
levels.securityFocus: Network segmentation, access control, data integrity, operator authentication
examples: SCADA dashboard showing all factory operations
HMI screen for power plant operators
Data historian recording all system events

levels.name: Operations/Systems Management
levels.description: Systems managing security, maintenance, and overall facility operations
levels.definition: Management systems that coordinate security policies, maintenance schedules, and operational decisions across the facility.
levels.explanation: This level handles the 'business' side of operations. It includes systems for managing security patches, scheduling maintenance, tracking assets, and enforcing policies. Security here means ensuring these management systems can't be manipulated to weaken security elsewhere.
levels.systems: Security management systems, asset management, patch management, log management
levels.securityFocus: Policy enforcement, audit logging, change management, vulnerability management
examples: System for managing security patches across all devices
Asset inventory tracking all equipment
Centralized logging system recording all security events

levels.name: Enterprise
levels.description: Organisation-wide systems integrating business and operational technology
levels.definition: The highest level where business systems (ERP, CRM) connect with operational systems, enabling organisation-wide decision-making.
levels.explanation: This is where the business office connects with the factory floor. Enterprise systems like ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning) integrate with operational systems. Security here means protecting the connection between business and operations, preventing attackers from using business systems to reach control systems.
levels.systems: ERP systems, business intelligence, corporate networks, cloud services
levels.securityFocus: Network segmentation from operations, data protection, access controls, incident response
examples: ERP system ordering materials based on production needs
Business analytics using operational data
Corporate email system (must be separated from operational systems)

securityLevels.title: ISA/IEC 62443 Security Levels (SL 0-4)
securityLevels.description: Five levels representing increasing protection against different threat profiles. Each level requires stronger security measures.

levels.name: SL 0
levels.title: No Protection
levels.explanation: This level means no cybersecurity measures are in place. It's rarely appropriate for modern systems but might apply to legacy systems with no network connection and no sensitive data.

levels.name: SL 1
levels.title: Basic Protection
levels.description: Protection against casual or accidental misuse
levels.threatProfile: Low resources, generic skills, low motivation
levels.explanation: Basic security measures protect against accidental misuse or casual attacks. Think of it like a 'Do Not Enter' sign - it stops honest people but not determined attackers.
examples: Default password policies
Basic user authentication
Simple network firewalls

levels.name: SL 2
levels.title: Intentional Violation Protection
levels.description: Protection against intentional violation using simple means
levels.threatProfile: Low resources, generic skills, low motivation
levels.explanation: SL 2 protects against attackers with basic skills and tools. It's like having a locked door and an alarm - it deters casual intruders but not professional thieves.
examples: Multi-factor authentication for critical systems
Network zones separated by firewalls
Encrypted communication between systems
Regular security patches

levels.name: SL 3
levels.title: Advanced Persistent Threat Protection
levels.description: Protection against advanced attacks using sophisticated means
levels.threatProfile: Medium to high resources, advanced skills, high motivation
levels.explanation: SL 3 is for critical systems that might be targeted by sophisticated attackers (like nation-states or organized crime). It requires advanced security measures and continuous monitoring.
characteristics: Regular security assessments and penetration testing
examples: Biometric authentication for critical access
Intrusion detection systems monitoring all traffic
Security Operations Center (SOC) monitoring 24/7
Regular penetration testing by security experts

levels.name: SL 4
levels.title: Maximum Protection
levels.description: Protection against the most sophisticated attacks
levels.threatProfile: Unlimited resources, expert skills, maximum motivation
levels.explanation: SL 4 is for the most critical systems - those that could cause massive harm if compromised. It assumes attackers have unlimited resources and expertise. Very few systems need SL 4.
characteristics: Regular security audits by external experts
examples: Nuclear power plant control systems
Critical national infrastructure
Systems protecting public safety

foundationalRequirements.title: Seven Foundational Requirements (FR)
foundationalRequirements.description: Core security functions that must be implemented at each security level. Each system gets a security level for each FR individually.

requirements.name: Identification & Authentication
requirements.description: Verifying who is accessing the system
requirements.explanation: Before a system trusts anyone, it needs to know who they are and verify their identity. This is like checking ID at a secure building entrance.
examples: Username and password login
Multi-factor authentication (password + phone code)
Biometric authentication (fingerprint, face recognition)
Certificate-based authentication for machines
requirements.examTips: IAC is the foundation - you can't control access if you don't know who's accessing

requirements.name: Use Control
requirements.description: Controlling what authorized users can do
requirements.explanation: Once you know who someone is, you control what they're allowed to do. A maintenance technician shouldn't be able to change production schedules.
examples: Role-based access control (different permissions for different jobs)
Limiting admin access to only those who need it
Preventing operators from changing security settings
Restricting data access based on job function

requirements.name: System Integrity
requirements.description: Ensuring data and systems haven't been tampered with
requirements.explanation: You need to know that the data and commands you're seeing are real and haven't been modified by an attacker. It's like verifying that a document hasn't been forged.
examples: Digital signatures on software updates
Checksums verifying file integrity
Monitoring for unauthorized changes to configuration
Detecting malware that modifies system files

requirements.name: Data Confidentiality
requirements.description: Protecting sensitive information from unauthorized disclosure
requirements.explanation: Some information is sensitive - trade secrets, personal data, security configurations. Confidentiality means only authorized people can see it.
examples: Encrypting sensitive data in transit
Encrypting data stored on disk
Limiting who can view security logs
Protecting passwords and encryption keys

requirements.name: Restrict Data Flow
requirements.description: Controlling where data can go in the network
requirements.explanation: Not all parts of a network should be able to communicate with each other. Restricting data flow prevents attackers from moving laterally through the network.
examples: Firewalls blocking unauthorized connections
Network segmentation keeping operations separate from business systems
Zones and conduits controlling communication paths
Preventing direct connection from internet to control systems

requirements.name: Timely Response
requirements.description: Detecting and responding to security incidents quickly
requirements.explanation: When an attack happens, speed matters. The faster you detect and respond, the less damage occurs.
examples: Intrusion detection systems alerting on suspicious activity
Security monitoring 24/7
Automated response to certain threats
Incident response procedures that activate quickly

requirements.name: Resource Availability
requirements.description: Ensuring systems and data are available when needed
requirements.explanation: A system that's always down due to attacks is as bad as one that's been compromised. Availability means systems work when they're supposed to.
examples: Redundant systems so one failure doesn't stop operations
DDoS protection preventing attackers from overwhelming systems
Backup systems that can take over if primary fails
Regular maintenance preventing unexpected downtime
